payload.headline: Microsoft steadies at 508.29 as outage reports linger; still a hold

summary.thesis: Microsoft's sales and margins are improving, but its free cash flow fell, so the price is fair only against its own history and expensive on cash flow.
summary.decision: Long-term hold, with new money only at the 486.0–491.22 support zone; no swing trade until price reaches that zone or clears 524.43.

payload.happening: Microsoft closed at 508.29, up 0.4%. That is still inside the 504.96–512.76 zone where it has traded lately, and below its 20-day average (526.09) and 50-day average (519.94). The news is about US tech outages: the Financial Times reported that outages were blamed on a rush to fix bugs found by AI, and CNBC reported that the administration says the incidents are not linked. A Verge headline about Satya Nadella's views on AGI is speculative. The next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
payload.business: Today's news changes sentiment and perhaps how much customers trust Microsoft's reliability. None of it is a filed fact about demand or margins. The business numbers come from the 2026-10-28 filing, and they are solid. Sales grew 18.8% from the same quarter last year, up from 18.3% two quarters ago. The operating margin (the share of sales left after running costs) rose to 47.1% from 46.27%. Net cash is 29.0B, and the share count fell 0.27% over the year. The weak spot is cash. Trailing free cash flow (cash left after investment spending) fell from 78.0B to 60.0B, and the filings note that each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, down from 51¢ three years ago. The real risk is that heavy spending does not turn into cash. Demand, margins and the balance sheet are not currently at risk. An outage story only matters if it turns into lost customers (general knowledge), and the data does not show that.

worth.text: The methods disagree sharply. A cash-flow model (DCF: the value today of future free cash flow, discounted at 10.1%) starts from the 60.0B of trailing free cash flow and gives 178.23 to 282.89 per share, with 214.86 in the middle. To justify today's price, that model needs free cash flow to start growing at 41.3% a year. Even 30% starting growth gives only 339.12. Against its own history, the stock is valued at a normal price-to-sales level. That gives 475.73 to 592.92, with 535.43 in the middle. The price-to-sales ratio of 10.9 sits at the 38th percentile of its own five-year range, but well above the 3.6 median for peers. On earnings, the price is 21.0 times next year's estimate of 24.2. The whole gap between methods comes down to one question: does today's depressed cash flow reflect the business, or a temporary spending peak? I use the own-history range of 475.73 to 535.43, because earnings and margins are rising while cash dips. I treat the DCF as the warning of what happens if that view is wrong.
worth.key_assumption: The spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash, so next-year earnings (estimate 24.2) are the right basis for value, not today's cash flow.

bull: Growth is speeding up, not slowing: quarterly sales grew 18.8% from a year ago, versus 18.3% two quarters ago.
Profitability is improving: operating margin rose to 47.1% from 46.27%, with a net margin of 41.17%.
Analysts keep raising forecasts: the next-year EPS estimate rose to 24.2 from 23.68 thirty days ago, up 2.2%.
bear: Free cash flow fell from 78.0B to 60.0B, and the price implies 41.3% starting cash-flow growth, which the model does not allow (it caps growth at 30%).
The price-to-sales ratio is 10.9, against a peer median of 3.6, which leaves little room for a miss.
Options are pricing fear: implied volatility is 50.7 against realized volatility of 37.4, and the market is in a tech downtrend, according to the macro read.

levels.what: Today's close sits inside the 475.73–535.43 fair range. There is no reason to sell, and no margin of safety for new money.
Top of the strongest support zone (486.0–491.22, 8 touches), near the 475.73 own-history low. Add here.
Middle of the own-history range. Above this the stock is not cheap even against its own past, and the case for trimming grows toward 592.92.

longterm.why: The business is improving, but two of the three valuation measures lean expensive because free cash flow is weak. The outage reports are about sentiment and do not change that balance.

swing.why: Price is stuck in a range, below the flat 20-day and 50-day averages, and resistance sits just above at 515.65–524.43. The cleaner setup is a test of support: entry at 491.22, stop at 480.69, first target at 515.65.

decision.timing: The 2027-02-19 options price a 13.8% move, and that expiry includes the 2027-01-27 report. So no new long-term money before that report's free cash flow figure, unless the price reaches 486.0–491.22.

change_mind: A close below 472.2, the bottom of the second support zone, would break the range and move the long-term call from hold to wait.
A close above 524.43, clearing resistance and the 20-day average of 526.09, would justify a swing entry, targeting 539.42.
If the 2027-01-27 report shows trailing free cash flow still below 60.0B, or quarterly EPS below the 4.94 consensus, I would lower the fair range toward the cash-flow values.
payload.what_changed: Unchanged: still a hold, confirmed by the close at 508.29 (up 0.4%) inside the 475.73–535.43 fair range, with the outage news staying a reported sentiment story and not a filed change to the business.
payload.label: Research, not advice.
